name: Political impotence and the retreat into private virtue
plain_explanation: When ordinary Greeks lost any real power over their own political fate -- power now lay with rival Macedonian generals and their armies -- serious-minded people stopped trying to reform the state and instead asked how an individual could stay virtuous, or at least undisturbed, in a world he could not control.
precise_definition: The historical-psychological condition, produced by the eclipse of the city-state, in which philosophy shifts its central question from 'how can we build a good state?' to 'how can the individual be happy or virtuous regardless of the state of the world?'
why_it_mattered: Russell presents this shift as the single most important consequence of the Hellenistic collapse for the history of philosophy, directly producing Cynicism, Scepticism, Epicureanism and (for most of its history) Stoicism, and eventually preparing the ground psychologically for Christianity's gospel of individual salvation.
historical_origin: Produced by the destruction of the old Greek City States' independence under Philip and Alexander and the ensuing Macedonian wars.
examples: The general shift, described at the chapter's close, of philosophy from 'a pillar of fire going before intrepid seekers after truth' to 'an ambulance picking up the weak and wounded'
competing_positions: The classical civic-minded philosophy of Plato and Aristotle, still oriented to reforming or ruling the state
influence_on_later_thinkers: Anticipates the entire subject matter of Chapters XXVI-XXVIII (Cynics, Sceptics, Epicureans, Stoics) and, ultimately, Christianity's this-worldly pessimism paired with other-worldly hope.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: This is Russell's central political-to-philosophical causal claim in the chapter.
